chapter1_statement:
Before the interviews take place, ethical considerations will be observed. Each participant will be informed of the purpose of the study, and their voluntary participation will be emphasized. A consent form will be provided, assuring them of confidentiality and the right to withdraw at any time. The interviews will be conducted in person on the availability of the participants. The discussions will focus on their experiences with counterfeit money, the specific difficulties they encounter in distinguishing real from fake bills, and any strategies they currently employ to verify authenticity. These conversations will be recorded with consent to ensure accurate transcription, and thematic analysis will later be applied to identify patterns in the responses. The insights gained from this phase will provide a strong foundation for understanding the real-world difficulties associated with counterfeit detection.
Following this, the study moves into the second phase, which involves identifying the key features necessary for the development of the BillSense mobile application. This phase consists of two parts, beginning with expert consultation through semi-structured interviews with professionals specializing in financial security and questioned document examiners (QDE). Their expertise is crucial in determining the essential security features that should be integrated into the mobile application. Participants will be carefully selected based on their professional background and experience in counterfeit detection. During the interviews, experts will be asked to share their knowledge on the most critical security elements of genuine banknotes and how digital tools can assist in verifying authenticity. The discussions will be recorded and transcribed, with thematic analysis applied to extract relevant insights.
Building upon the expert recommendations, the study will proceed to the next stage, where an initial prototype of the BillSense mobile application will be developed. Once the prototype is ready, the same financial security experts who participated in the first round of interviews will be invited to test the application. This process allows them to assess the app’s ability to detect counterfeit bills and determine whether it meets the required security standards. During the testing session, they will use the app to scan real and counterfeit banknotes, evaluating its accuracy, functionality, and overall usability. Their feedback will be gathered through follow-up discussions, focusing on any necessary improvements before wider usability testing is conducted. The results of this phase will inform further refinements to the system, ensuring that the app effectively addresses counterfeit detection concerns.
The final phase of data collection shifts towards evaluating the acceptability of the BillSense mobile application. At this stage, the respondents will include market vendors, small business owners or cashiers, and consumers, being the primary users of the proposed application. To identify the participants, a quota sampling method will be applied, dividing the participants into distinct groups based on their role in handling and verifying banknotes.
During acceptability testing, respondents will be asked to perform predefined tasks using the BillSense app, such as scanning a banknote and interpreting the application’s feedback regarding authenticity. To systematically assess the user experience, the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) will be administered after the testing session. This standardized questionnaire is widely used in acceptability and usability research to measure the perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of the mobile application. The survey responses will be analyzed quantitatively, providing numerical insights into the app’s acceptance level. Additionally, participants may be asked follow-up questions to capture qualitative feedback on specific features or areas that need improvement. Once all three phases of data collection are completed, the study will proceed with data analysis.
Treatment of the Data
Given the mixed-method research design, distinct analytical techniques will be employed for each type of data, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the challenges in counterfeit detection, the key features of an effective mobile application, and the usability of the developed BillSense system.
THEMATIC ANALYSIS. For the qualitative data obtained from semi-structured interviews in SOP 1 and SOP 2, thematic analysis will be utilized. This approach, as described by Braun and Clarke (2006), involves identifying, analyzing, and reporting patterns (themes) within the data. The recorded interviews will first be transcribed, after which a coding process will be conducted to categorize responses based on recurring ideas, challenges, and recommendations. The emerging themes will provide deeper insights into the experiences of individuals who frequently handle cash, the difficulties they encounter in counterfeit detection, and the expert perspectives on the essential features for the mobile application. This method ensures that the qualitative data is systematically examined, allowing for meaningful interpretations that contribute to the study’s findings.
DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS. For the acceptability testing conducted in SOP 3, descriptive statistical analysis will be applied. This includes calculating the mean and standard deviation for the constructs of Perceived Usefulness (PU) and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU). The mean will give an overall sense of how respondents rate the proposed app’s usefulness and ease of use. The standard deviation will show how varied or consistent the perceptions are across participants. A low standard deviation indicates that most respondents have similar views, while a high standard deviation shows that opinions are more spread out. Additionally, frequency distribution will be used to show how often each response was selected for each item on the Likert scale (e.g., Strongly Disagree, Disagree, Neutral, Agree, Strongly Agree). This will help identify if most participants perceive the app as useful and easy to use, or if opinions are more divided. Finally, the mode will be used to determine the most common response for each construct, providing insight into the general sentiment toward the app's perceived usefulness and ease of use (Sekaran et al., 2016). These descriptive statistics will offer an overview of how the app is viewed by the target users and serve as a foundation for further analysis.
TRIANGULATION. For the final interpretation of the data, triangulation will be employed to integrate the qualitative insights from interviews with the quantitative usability metrics. Triangulation, as discussed by Denzin (1978), enhances the validity of research findings by comparing multiple sources of data. The qualitative themes will be analyzed alongside the numerical usability scores to determine whether the challenges and features identified in the earlier stages align with user experiences during testing. This approach ensures that the study’s conclusions are well-supported by both empirical evidence and real-world user feedback.
Through these analytical methods, the study will provide a well-rounded evaluation of the BillSense application. The thematic analysis of user challenges and expert recommendations will guide the interpretation of qualitative data, while statistical analysis of usability test results will ensure objective validation of the system’s effectiveness. By employing a rigorous approach to data treatment, the study ensures that its findings contribute meaningfully to the development of an accessible and reliable counterfeit detection solution.

This paradigm of the study explains the research process by outlining the steps involved. It begins with gathering data from end users to identify challenges in counterfeit detection, followed by expert insights to recommend key features that should be integrated into the mobile application being developed. Using a design thinking approach, the research defines the problem, develops a prototype, and iterates based on user feedback. This ensures that BillSense is a well-researched, user-friendly tool that effectively addresses the identified challenges in detecting counterfeit banknotes.

chapter1_background:
Counterfeit currency has long been a formidable challenge to financial systems worldwide, threatening economic stability, eroding public trust, and facilitating illicit activities. The ability of counterfeiters to replicate banknotes with increasing sophistication has been exacerbated by advancements in printing and scanning technologies, making traditional detection methods inadequate in many cases. As a result, nations across the globe continue to grapple with counterfeiting threats, despite significant efforts to enhance security features and detection systems. The global prevalence of counterfeit money necessitates the continuous evolution of anti-counterfeiting measures, integrating technological innovations with robust legal and economic strategies to safeguard financial integrity (Srilatha, 2024; Upadhyaya, 2018).
Counterfeit currency has historically been a tool of economic warfare, as illustrated by Germany's Operation Bernhard in World War II, which aimed to destabilize enemy economies by inundating them with fake banknotes (Dalimunthe, 2023). The Nazi regime's objective was to saturate allied nations with counterfeit British pounds and US dollars, with the goal of inciting inflation and eroding financial stability (Burger, 2009). At the Sachsenhausen concentration camp, 144 inmates were compelled to create counterfeit notes valued in the billions, which were so expertly crafted that even the Bank of England found it challenging to identify them as forgeries (Burger, 2009). This approach highlighted how extensive counterfeiting could be weaponized to induce inflation and financial damage, a tactic that persists in contemporary conflicts. For example, reports suggest that Iran participated in counterfeiting the Yemeni rial during Yemen’s civil war to destabilize the nation’s economy (Crespo, 2020). The influx of counterfeit money increases the money supply without a corresponding rise in economic output, resulting in artificial inflation and diminished purchasing power (Sharma, 2022 & Shaik, 2024). These examples illustrate the profound geopolitical consequences of counterfeit currency, extending beyond simple financial fraud and emphasizing the need for effective global countermeasures.
Globally, counterfeiting continues to be a significant challenge, especially in areas where high-value currencies are prevalent. The U.S. dollar and the Euro, recognized as the most commonly utilized currencies in global trade (De Best, 2025), have become prime targets for counterfeit operations. The U.S. dollar is particularly susceptible due to its role as the world's reserve currency, with evidence showing that counterfeit $20 bills are a frequent source of financial losses (Judson, 2003). Likewise, the Euro, particularly in higher denominations such as €50 and €100, has encountered serious counterfeiting risks, intensified by its widespread use across borders (Gh, 2024). The increase in counterfeit currency production is largely due to the high-value denominations that offer greater profits for counterfeiters (Anderson, 2007).
In Southern Asia, the counterfeiting of the Indian Rupee, especially the ₹500 and ₹2000 notes, is viewed through a different lens, as it is closely tied to the effectiveness of the currency's security features rather than being seen as a high-value currency. This growing trend of counterfeit currency presents a considerable threat to the region's financial stability, despite government measures such as demonetization (Teja, 2024; Colaco, 2021).
To highlight the relationship between the ease of counterfeiting and the effectiveness of a bill's security features, The Hindu News (2025) reported that the 500 and 2,000 Indian rupee banknotes, introduced in 2016, incorporate various security measures aimed at thwarting counterfeiting. Nevertheless, these denominations are still vulnerable to imitation, which is why their features must be updated every three to four years. Both denominations include several common security elements, such as a see-through register, latent image, micro lettering, security thread, watermark, intaglio printing, and color-changing ink. According to India Today (2017), investigations into counterfeit currency found that 11 out of 17 security features had been effectively replicated by counterfeiters, including the transparent area, watermark, emblem, and color-shifting thread. The government recognizes that the failure to regularly update security features contributes to the ease with which counterfeiters can study and reproduce the notes. Coupled with the static security features is the inadequacy of a counterfeit detection system, doubling the risk of the notes from being replicated. In India, these detection mechanisms have only achieved an 81% accuracy rate when assessing ₹2000 notes, indicating a pressing need for more effective solutions (Teja, 2024).
In contrast, some currencies have managed to maintain lower counterfeiting rates due to their advanced security features and stringent enforcement measures. For instance, Kazakhstan’s Tenge benefits from intricate banknote designs, legislative deterrents, and public education campaigns that make counterfeiting significantly more difficult (Sembekova, 2024). The National Bank of Kazakhstan integrates advanced security features into Tenge banknotes to deter counterfeiters. Specifically, the 10,000 Tenge note includes a two-tone security thread appearing as dotted lines on the surface and exhibits a dynamic pulsating effect of interacting blue and purple colors when tilted. Additionally, it features a three-dimensional image of a stylized snow leopard that transforms into an ornament with dynamic rays spreading outward upon rotation. Other features include a color-changing window revealing a mountain peak silhouette shifting from gold to blue and a spark element displaying a three-dimensional image that changes color from gold to jade when tilted. Furthermore, the 5,000 Tenge banknote incorporates a two-color security thread creating a dynamic pulsating effect of red and blue colors when tilted. It also features a volumetric image of the Berkut artifact, showcasing a transition effect from the denomination figure to an ornament, accompanied by dynamic solar sign rays diverging sideways (National Bank of Kazakhstan, 2025). These advanced security features greatly contributed to the relatively low statistics on counterfeit currency circulation and production of Tenge (Tengre News, 2025).
On the other hand, the Chinese Yuan (RMB) 50 denomination employs fiber optic diamond probes to visualize weak magnetic fields in its anti-counterfeiting strip, a feature that makes replication highly challenging (Zhao, 2024). Historically, counterfeit currency has posed a significant issue in China, particularly in 2014 when law enforcement seized counterfeit banknotes amounting to 532 million yuan, reflecting a 25% increase from previous years (CTGN America, 2015). In response, the People’s Bank of China launched a new 100-yuan banknote that incorporated enhanced security features, including color-changing ink and improved machine-readable elements, with the aim of reducing the incidence of counterfeiting (The Beijinger, 2016). As a result of these initiatives, the rate of counterfeit currency in China was deemed moderate compared to other major currencies, despite its previous status as a significant concern. However, in March 2016, a counterfeit version of the new 100-yuan note was uncovered, indicating that counterfeiters were still attempting to replicate even the latest designs (The Beijinger, 2016). Two primary factors contributing to this ongoing issue are the reliance on cash and advancements in counterfeiting technology. China's heavy dependence on cash transactions, particularly in rural regions, fosters an environment conducive to counterfeiting (BytesCare, 2024). Despite the growth of digital payment methods, cash continues to be widely used, providing counterfeiters with numerous opportunities to circulate fake banknotes. Additionally, counterfeiters have increasingly leveraged advanced technologies to create counterfeit notes that can evade detection by standard verification machines. This was exemplified in 2016 when Chinese police discovered counterfeit notes so expertly crafted that they bypassed detection devices and were accepted by unsuspecting individuals (Kwong, 2016).
The global shift to polymer banknotes has significantly contributed to the fight against counterfeiting. Nations including the United Kingdom, Australia, and Mexico have embraced polymer materials, which provide greater durability and incorporate advanced security elements such as transparent windows and optically variable devices (OVDs) that are challenging to reproduce (Hardwick, 2001). While the primary goal of implementing polymer banknotes was to bolster security and minimize counterfeiting, similar to the situation in China, counterfeiters have sought to replicate these unique security features through advanced printing methods, highlighting the necessity for ongoing innovation (Wang, 2021).
In Australia, the transition to polymer banknotes in 1996 resulted in a notable decrease in counterfeiting incidents. However, as time progressed, counterfeiters adapted their methods, leading to a consistent increase in counterfeit detections by 2010. By 2015, polymer notes had become the primary material used in counterfeiting, with approximately 60% of counterfeit notes printed on polymer by 2021, a significant rise from just over 20% a decade earlier (Reserve Bank of Australia, 2019). In the United Kingdom, the transition commenced in 2016 with the introduction of the 5-pound note, followed by additional notes in 2017, 2020, and the 50-pound note in 2021. Prior to this transition, the UK faced counterfeiting rates in the millions, and the implementation of polymer notes is anticipated to have curbed counterfeiting due to their superior security features (Reserve Bank of Australia, 2019). These trends illustrate that while polymer banknotes mark a considerable advancement in the fight against counterfeiting, they remain vulnerable to the evolving strategies of criminals (Solomon, 2014).
The evolution of counterfeiting techniques has been closely linked to advancements in printing, scanning, and manufacturing technologies. In the past, counterfeiting demanded specialized tools and knowledge; however, the rise of consumer-grade devices has significantly reduced the entry barriers for criminals (Pilania, 2016). Today, the availability of high-resolution color printers, laser scanners, and even 3D printing technology allows counterfeiters to reproduce complex security features with remarkable precision (Laavanya, 2019). Modern digital printers, including inkjet and laser types, can accurately replicate the detailed designs and colors present on banknotes, while software like Photoshop facilitates the meticulous alteration of images to imitate security features. This accessibility has made counterfeiting feasible for individuals with limited skills, contributing to the increased circulation of counterfeit currency (Chaban, 2022).
In addition to enhancing the security features of currency, economic and legal strategies are vital in the fight against counterfeit money. The presence of fake currency disrupts financial transactions, undermines the value of legitimate currency, and exacerbates inflation, especially in economies already facing issues of corruption and black-market activities (Alekhya, 2014). Counterfeit operations often support larger criminal networks, including those involved in financing terrorism, which further destabilizes economies (Sharma, 2022). In response, governments have enacted strict penalties for counterfeiting. For instance, Indonesia imposes sentences of up to 15 years for counterfeiters under Article 244 of its Criminal Code (Harefa, 2023), while Kazakhstan has introduced comprehensive legislative measures along with public awareness campaigns to bolster financial security (Sembekova, 2024). The historical context of robust anti-counterfeiting actions, such as the U.S. Secret Service's efforts against counterfeiters in the 19th century, underscores the necessity of coordinated enforcement initiatives (Gollin, 2009).
Despite these measures, counterfeiters continue to thrive largely because they take advantage of the public's limited ability to recognize fake currency. Although banknotes are designed with sophisticated security features to combat counterfeiting, their success is contingent upon users being able to identify these elements. The widespread lack of knowledge and skill in detecting counterfeit money heightens the risk of fraudulent transactions and can lead to economic instability (Horst, 2021 & DN, 2024). This challenge is further intensified by advancements in printing and scanning technologies, which allow counterfeiters to reproduce these security features with remarkable accuracy (Viraktamath, 2021 & Shaikh, 2024).
As counterfeiting methods advance, conventional detection techniques struggle to keep up, facing notable challenges in terms of accuracy, scalability, and adaptability. Traditional methods for identifying counterfeit banknotes primarily rely on manual inspection and specialized tools to evaluate embedded security features (Dri Mark, 2021). These methods include tactile assessments, visual inspections, ultraviolet (UV) light scanning, counterfeit detection pens, and machine-assisted detection technologies (Shokeen, 2022).
Manual inspection entails assessing the texture and visual elements of a banknote. Genuine currency is typically printed on unique substrates, such as cotton-based paper or polymer, imparting a distinct tactile feel (van der Horst & Theeuwes, 2020). Experienced cash handlers can often detect counterfeits by noting deviations in texture. However, this technique necessitates considerable expertise and can be unreliable, especially as counterfeiters refine their replication methods (National Research Council, 2006). Visual examination entails scrutinizing visible security features like watermarks, color-shifting inks, and intricate designs. While effective to an extent, this approach demands familiarity with the specific features of each denomination and is susceptible to human error. Additionally, wear and tear can obscure these features, making detection more challenging (Patel & Patel, 2023).
Ultraviolet (UV) light scanning is another commonly employed method. UV scanners detect fluorescent elements embedded in banknotes that remain hidden under normal lighting but glow when exposed to UV light (National Research Council, 2006). Although this method offers a rapid verification process, its reliability has limitations. Advanced counterfeiters have created ways to replicate these fluorescent characteristics, enabling some counterfeit bills to evade detection (Patel & Patel, 2023). Additionally, UV scanners may fail to identify high-quality fakes that do not exhibit UV features but successfully imitate other characteristics of authentic banknotes (Shokeen, 2022).
Counterfeit detection pens, containing iodine-based ink that reacts with starches found in regular paper, are also widely used. Since genuine currency-grade paper does not contain these starches, the ink leaves a dark stain on counterfeit notes (Dri Mark, 2021). However, this method is flawed as some counterfeiters use starch-free paper, rendering the pen ineffective. Conversely, legitimate banknotes contaminated with starch through handling may yield false positives, leading to unnecessary confusion (National Research Council, 2006).
To enhance accuracy, financial institutions often employ machine-assisted detection technologies that analyze multiple security features, including magnetic properties, infrared markings, and microprinting (Patel & Patel, 2023). Although these advanced machines enhance detection rates, their high cost makes them impractical for small businesses or individual users. Moreover, as counterfeiters increasingly employ sophisticated printing and scanning technologies, even these advanced machines struggle to differentiate high-quality fakes from authentic banknotes (Shokeen, 2022).
The limitations of traditional counterfeit detection methods are evident in their susceptibility to human error, accessibility issues, and lack of adaptability. Manual inspections, despite being widely practiced, are inherently subjective and prone to mistakes, particularly under time constraints or when handling large volumes of cash (van der Horst & Theeuwes, 2020). High-end counterfeit detection machines, though effective, are costly and often remain exclusive to banks and financial institutions, limiting access for small businesses and everyday consumers (Dri Mark, 2021). Moreover, traditional methods struggle to keep pace with evolving counterfeiting techniques, as criminals continuously refine their methods, incorporating high-resolution printing and advanced scanning technologies to produce deceptive counterfeits (Shokeen, 2022). This underscores the urgent need for more automated, adaptable, and efficient counterfeit detection systems that integrate advanced technologies (Patel & Patel, 2023).
To address these shortcomings, researchers have explored image processing techniques as a means of improving counterfeit detection accuracy. Image processing methods, including edge detection, bit-plane slicing, and image segmentation, offer improved feature extraction capabilities, allowing for the identification of intricate security features such as watermarks and optically variable devices (Ballado, 2015; Viraktamath, 2021). Generally, image processing techniques are essential for extracting and analyzing features that differentiate genuine currency from counterfeit. Key methods include image segmentation, grayscale conversion, and filtering to collectively enhance the detection process. The image segmentation technique isolates specific regions of a banknote such as watermarks or security threads, enabling focused analysis (Alshayeji, 2015 & Srinivas, 2023). Grayscale conversion, on the other hand, converts images to grayscale to simplify processing through reduced computational complexity (Shiby, 2021 & Desai, 2024). Filtering techniques under image processing would smoothen the image, removing the noise and artifacts which is particularly helpful in improving the clarity of the micro-letters and security threads (Viraktamath, 2021). These methods are often combined in automated systems to improve detection speed and reliability (Sundravadivelu, 2024).
Edge detection is an essential method in image processing that facilitates the recognition of boundaries and features by concentrating on regions with significant intensity changes. Among the various algorithms available, the Canny Edge Detection technique is particularly esteemed for its accuracy and reliability in identifying both strong and weak edges (Canny, 1986 & Maini, 2004). The Canny algorithm consists of five main phases: noise reduction, gradient calculation, non-maximum suppression, double thresholding, and edge tracking (Canny, 1986 & Kamanga, 2017). Initially, noise reduction employs a Gaussian filter to smooth the image and reduce noise interference. Next, gradient calculation assesses the intensity gradients to determine the strength and direction of edges. In the non-maximum suppression phase, only the thinnest edges are preserved by eliminating non-maximum gradient values. During double thresholding, edges are categorized into strong and weak based on specific intensity thresholds. Finally, edge tracking ensures that weak edges connected to strong edges are maintained (Canny, 1986 & Kamanga, 2017). In the context of counterfeit currency detection, Canny edge detection is particularly effective at revealing complex features like watermarks and micro-lettering. Nonetheless, it is highly susceptible to noise and variations in banknote designs, which may result in false positives or negatives, thereby impacting the overall accuracy of detection (Alshayeji, 2015).
Bit-plane slicing similarly improves feature extraction by dividing grayscale images into binary layers, enhancing clarity; however, it requires substantial computational resources, which can result in delays for real-time applications (Alshayeji, 2015). This technique is particularly effective in identifying subtle security features in counterfeit currency detection. By breaking down an image into binary planes, it allows for the examination of individual bits that contribute to the overall structure and detail of the image (Hernandez, 2008 & Alshayeji, 2015). Higher-order bit planes often uncover vital features such as watermarks, microprinting, and fine edges, which are crucial for differentiating between genuine and counterfeit notes. The primary benefits of bit-plane slicing include improved feature visibility (Hernandez, 2008), enhanced edge detection that accelerates and refines edge identification (Alshayeji, 2015), and its adaptability for both grayscale and RGB images (Hernandez, 2008).
Image segmentation further isolates specific areas of interest, such as security threads and holograms, for detailed analysis. Despite its potential, segmentation struggles with complex backgrounds and overlapping features, which can hinder detection accuracy (Sundravadivelu, 2024). These challenges indicate that while image processing provides an improvement over traditional methods, further optimization is needed to enhance speed and reliability in counterfeit detection.
To improve the weaknesses of conventional image processing methods, there has been extensive research into machine learning and deep learning techniques, which have shown remarkable progress in detecting counterfeit currency. Machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence, allows systems to learn and enhance their performance through experience without the need for explicit programming. It emphasizes the creation of algorithms capable of analyzing data, learning from it, and making predictions based on that information (Holdsworth & Scapicchio, 2024). Deep learning, a more specialized area within machine learning, employs multilayered neural networks to replicate the complex decision-making abilities of the human brain. These deep neural networks can autonomously identify and learn intricate patterns within vast datasets, making them especially effective for applications such as image and speech recognition (Holdsworth & Scapicchio, 2024).
Machine learning approach relies on feature extraction, in which, experts manually identify and extract relevant features from currency images, such as color histograms, edge patterns, texture descriptors, and watermark presence. Once features are extracted, algorithms like Support Vector Machines (SVM), Decision Trees, or Random Forests are trained on labeled datasets of genuine and counterfeit notes to learn distinguishing patterns (Holdsworth & Scapicchio, 2024). The advantages of using the machine learning approach includes its heightened effectivity in dealing with smaller datasets and requiring less computational power. The disadvantage would include the heavy dependence on the quality of manually extracted features. Deep learning on the other hand, particularly Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), automatically learn hierarchical features directly from raw images, eliminating the need for manual feature extraction.
In the context of machine and deep learning methodologies, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Support Vector Machines (SVMs), and Random Forest classifiers have been thoroughly investigated for their effectiveness in analyzing security features with high precision (Gh, 2024; Pathak, 2024). CNNs are particularly proficient in feature extraction and classification, achieving notable accuracy levels. However, their effectiveness is significantly influenced by the availability of large and varied datasets, which can be challenging to acquire. A lack of sufficient data can result in overfitting, making it difficult for models to perform well on new counterfeit samples (Srivastava, 2024). Additionally, CNNs demand considerable computational power and lengthy training periods, which can limit their practicality for real-time applications (Pachón, 2021). Conversely, SVMs and Random Forest classifiers present feasible options for smaller datasets, although they face challenges related to scalability and feature complexity. SVMs are especially affected by the size and diversity of the dataset, which can compromise their accuracy, while Random Forest classifiers, despite their robustness, can become computationally intensive when handling large datasets (Agasti, 2024). These challenges underscore the necessity for enhanced algorithms and better-quality datasets to improve counterfeit detection systems.
A comparative evaluation of current counterfeit detection methods indicates that machine learning techniques consistently surpass traditional and image-processing methods in terms of both accuracy and scalability. Conventional approaches, such as manual inspections and UV scanners, are limited by human error and their inability to identify advanced counterfeits (Alekhya, 2014; Padmaja, 2021). While image processing methods enhance feature extraction, they are plagued by sensitivity to noise and require significant computational power (Ballado, 2015; Sundravadivelu, 2024). In contrast, machine learning methods, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Support Vector Machines (SVMs), show superior accuracy, with CNN models achieving counterfeit detection rates as high as 98.5% (Gh, 2024). Nonetheless, machine learning approaches face challenges related to dataset limitations, the potential for overfitting, and the demand for extensive computational resources (Srivastava, 2024; Pachón, 2021). These insights highlight the need for the development of more efficient and flexible solutions to enhance counterfeit detection technologies.
Emerging technologies, such as hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and transfer learning, present promising avenues for overcoming the limitations of current detection methods. Hyperspectral imaging captures electromagnetic data across multiple wavelengths, enabling the identification of subtle security features that are difficult to replicate, such as watermarks and holograms. A snapshot-based HSI algorithm, for example, has demonstrated high efficiency in distinguishing genuine and counterfeit Taiwanese banknotes by analyzing mean gray values in specific wavelength ranges (Mukundan, 2023). In addition, hyperspectral imaging systems can operate in low-light environments using active illumination, ensuring consistent spectral data acquisition (Tang, 2023).
Similarly, transfer learning leverages pre-trained models to enhance detection accuracy while reducing computational demands. Research utilizing MobileNetv2 has achieved a mean Average Precision (mAP) of over 92% for detecting counterfeit Philippine banknotes, showcasing its effectiveness in feature extraction while maintaining lightweight computational requirements (Goma, 2024). Moreover, a transfer-learned CNN model trained on diverse datasets has exhibited higher accuracy in real-time counterfeit detection, underscoring its adaptability to evolving counterfeiting techniques (Srilatha, 2024).
The need for advanced counterfeit detection is particularly relevant in the Philippines, where the evolution of currency reflects ongoing efforts to enhance security and durability. The rollout of new banknotes in the Philippines in late 2024 highlights the country’s commitment to strengthening financial security and combating counterfeit currency. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has emphasized that the transition to polymer banknotes is designed to minimize counterfeiting and enhance financial safety. As stated by the BSP (2024), polymer banknotes are smarter than paper banknotes because they incorporate more sophisticated security features, making them significantly harder to replicate.
The history of Philippine currency reflects not only the country’s economic and political journey but also the continuous battle against counterfeiting. As money evolved, so did fraudulent attempts to replicate it, necessitating advancements in security features and materials. Before the arrival of Spanish colonizers, early Filipinos used gold as a medium of exchange, including Piloncitos — small, rounded gold pieces – and Barter Rings. Due to gold’s inherent value and difficulty to forge, counterfeiting was virtually non-existent. However, as trade expanded and standardized currency systems emerged, the risk of fake money increased. During the Spanish colonial period, silver coins such as Macuquinas and Spanish pesos were introduced. These were often subject to "clipping," where individuals shaved off small amounts of silver from the edges of the coins before passing them off as full-value currency. In response, the Spanish authorities introduced milled-edge coins, a security measure that made tampering more detectable (Banko Sentral ng Pilipinas [BSP], n.d.). Counterfeit coins, often of lower silver content, also circulated, prompting the Spanish government to introduce standardized coin designs and stamping to deter forgeries.
With the increasing integration of the Philippine economy into global trade, counterfeit banknotes started to emerge, especially following the issuance of the first paper currency by El Banco Español Filipino de Isabel II in the 19th century. The reproduction of paper money proved to be simpler than that of metal coins, prompting the implementation of watermarks and security threads as measures against counterfeiting (BSP, n.d.).
During the Philippine Revolution against Spanish rule, the Republika Filipina pesos were created as a representation of independence. These banknotes were typically either handwritten or produced using rudimentary printing techniques, which made them susceptible to forgery by both revolutionaries and opportunists. The tumultuous nature of the era further exacerbated the devaluation of currency and the spread of unauthorized replicas. With the onset of American governance, the Philippine Peso (PHP) was introduced in 1903, signifying a transition to more secure printing methods. The Americans, leveraging their sophisticated banking infrastructure, introduced enhancements such as intricate engravings and consistent paper quality. However, despite these advancements, counterfeit notes continued to circulate, especially in rural regions where banking regulations were not as rigorously applied.
The Japanese occupation during World War II resulted in one of the most severe instances of hyperinflation and counterfeit currency in the history of the Philippines. The military currency issued by the Japanese, notoriously known as “Mickey Mouse” money, was produced in large quantities with few security measures, leading to widespread counterfeiting. Both ordinary citizens and resistance factions began creating their own versions of this currency, which further diminished its value. By the conclusion of the war, the Japanese peso had lost nearly all its worth, highlighting how ineffective anti-counterfeiting strategies can lead to economic collapse (BSP, n.d.).
Following independence, the newly formed Central Bank of the Philippines (now known as BSP) assumed responsibility for currency production, focusing on enhancing security features to combat counterfeiting. The English Series (1949–1969) introduced intricate line patterns and specialized inks to make forgery more difficult. Subsequent series, including the Pilipino Series (1969–1973) and the New Design Series (1973–1993), further advanced security measures by adding watermarks, security fibers, and intaglio printing—methods that remain in use today to fight counterfeiting. Nevertheless, as counterfeiters evolved their techniques, the BSP was compelled to continuously update its security features.
The introduction of the New Generation Currency (NGC) series in 2010 represented a major leap forward in anti-counterfeiting technology. These banknotes incorporated ten distinct security features, including a unique texture of the security paper, embossed prints, a watermark, security fibers, an asymmetrical serial number, a see-through mark, a security thread, concealed value, optically variable ink, and an optically variable device patch (BSP, 2010). However, despite these advancements, counterfeiters were still able to produce high-quality fakes, often taking advantage of gaps in public knowledge. The Enhanced NGC series addressed this issue by adding two additional features: tactile marks to assist the visually impaired in distinguishing between different banknote denominations and an improved value panel for the 1000-peso and 500-peso notes.
The shift to polymer banknotes in 2022 represented the most advanced countermeasure against counterfeiting to date. Polymer notes, starting with the 1,000-peso denomination featuring the Philippine eagle, are more durable and incorporate cutting-edge security features such as transparent windows, holograms, and color-shifting inks, making them significantly harder to replicate (BSP, 2022). Countries that have adopted polymer currency, such as Australia and Canada, have reported substantial reductions in counterfeit incidents (Reserve Bank of Australia, 2021).
While the country’s currency has undergone several transformations — from gold barter rings to modern polymer banknotes — counterfeiters have continuously adapted, challenging the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) and law enforcement agencies to enhance security measures. The history of counterfeiting in the Philippines provides critical insights into the economic, legal, and technological responses to this ongoing financial threat.
The earliest documented case of counterfeiting in the Philippines occurred on January 16, 1903, when Alfonso P. Gardner and his accomplices were accused of falsifying U.S. silver certificates in Manila. They manipulated genuine one-dollar bills by altering the denomination to make them appear as ten-dollar bills. This deception led to their conviction under Article 289 of the Penal Code, which penalized the falsification of banknotes authorized by law (People v. Gardner, 1904). Another early case occurred in 1941 when Nicasio Barraquia attempted to exchange a counterfeit ten-peso banknote at a post office in Calamba, Laguna. He claimed he had received the bill in a gambling game, but due to insufficient evidence proving his knowledge of its falsity, the court acquitted him (People v. Barraquia, 1946). These early cases highlight not only the presence of counterfeit money but also the legal challenges in prosecuting individuals accused of using fraudulent currency.
One of the most notorious modern counterfeiting cases took place in 2005 when authorities seized over PHP 3 million worth of fake Philippine banknotes. The counterfeiters had successfully replicated PHP 1,000 bills with near-authentic security features, making them difficult to detect with the naked eye. Investigations revealed that the operation used high-resolution digital printing techniques and imported materials to mimic the appearance of genuine currency. This case underscored the growing sophistication of counterfeiters and the need for enhanced security features in Philippine banknotes (Philippine Daily Inquirer, 2005).
In Gacasan v. People of the Philippines (2023), the Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Allan Gacasan, who was caught selling counterfeit banknotes in Bukidnon. The court ruled that intent to distribute fraudulent currency constituted a criminal act under Article 168 of the Revised Penal Code, reinforcing the state’s firm stance against counterfeiting (SC Judiciary, 2023). Meanwhile, cases such as Gallano y Obrar v. People of the Philippines (2024) demonstrated the importance of proving mens rea (criminal intent) in counterfeit currency offenses. Gallano was acquitted after being accused of using a counterfeit PHP 1,000 bill, as there was no conclusive proof that he knowingly possessed fake money. Such rulings highlight the complexities involved in prosecuting counterfeit currency crimes, especially when intent is difficult to establish.
In recent years, the incidence of counterfeit currency has varied, often paralleling advancements in counterfeiting technology. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) reported a 7% rise in counterfeit banknotes in 2021 compared to the prior year, with Metro Manila, CALABARZON, Central Visayas, and Central Luzon representing 83.5% of these cases (BSP, 2022). This increase was linked to the revival of cash transactions after pandemic-related lockdowns and the adoption of advanced scanning and printing methods by counterfeiters. In response, law enforcement ramped up anti-counterfeiting efforts, resulting in numerous arrests and the confiscation of significant quantities of counterfeit banknotes. In 2023, the BSP executed 11 major enforcement operations, leading to the apprehension of 19 individuals and the filing of 25 criminal charges (PhilStar, 2024). Despite the law enforcement efforts coupled with the advancements of the financial institutions to curb the cases of counterfeiting in the country, it persists as an issue both in urban and rural areas because of the users’ level of skill in identifying counterfeit from genuine (Dalugdog & Sancon, 2024).
At present, to combat counterfeiting, various detection methods have been developed, ranging from traditional manual inspections to technologically advanced solutions. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has integrated multiple layers of security features into the New Generation Currency (NGC) banknotes, making it easier for the public to recognize genuine bills while increasing the difficulty and cost of counterfeiting. Manual inspection of the end users will encompass the first layer of security features. This relies on the principles of “look,” “feel,” and “tilt,” allowing cash handlers to detect security features through simple observation and touch. One of the most noticeable features is the embossed print, where the raised texture of the ink, combined with the cotton-based paper quality, gives the banknote a distinct tactile feel. This can be felt over the words “REPUBLIKA NG PILIPINAS,” the denominational value, the signatures, and the value panels. Another distinguishing element is the asymmetric serial number, located at the lower left and upper right corners of the note, where the alphanumeric characters increase in font size and thickness, ensuring uniqueness.
In addition to these, security fibers embedded within the paper are visible as scattered red and blue fibers across both the front and back of the note. A watermark, featuring a shadow image of the portrait along with the denominational value, appears when the note is held up against the light. Similarly, a see-through mark, found at the lower right corner, contains a pre-Hispanic Baybayin script spelling “PILIPINO,” which aligns perfectly when viewed against the light. Another important feature is the concealed value, which appears only when the note is rotated at a 45-degree angle, revealing the denomination superimposed on a smaller version of the portrait.
To further bolster security, a vertical security thread is incorporated across various denominations. In the 20- and 50-peso notes, this thread is embedded within the paper and becomes visible when held up to the light. In contrast, the 100-, 200-, 500-, and 1000-peso notes feature a stitch-like metallic thread that spans the width of the bill, changing color from red to green and displaying the text “BSP” along with the denomination in a repeated pattern. Higher denominations include additional advanced security features, such as the optically variable device (OVD) patch, which is exclusive to the 500- and 1000-peso notes. This reflective foil patch changes color from red to green when tilted 90 degrees and showcases an image of a Blue-naped Parrot on the 500-peso note and a clam with a South Sea pearl on the 1000-peso note. Additionally, the 1000-peso note incorporates optically variable ink (OVI), where the embossed denomination in the lower right corner shifts from green to blue based on the angle of view.
In addition to the easily identifiable security features, there are further verification layers available for professionals and authorities. Bank tellers and cash handlers can utilize magnifying glasses or ultraviolet (UV) light to reveal fluorescent security elements and microprinting that are not visible to the naked eye. Certain hidden security features are specifically designated for the internal verification processes of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), while forensic-level security components necessitate laboratory analysis and specialized tools to confirm a banknote's authenticity, especially in legal contexts.
Manual examination of banknotes is a common technique for identifying counterfeit currency. However, its success largely hinges on the user's expertise and their ability to distinguish real banknotes from counterfeit ones, rendering it a less dependable method for the general populace. Research indicates that while individuals can detect counterfeit banknotes at a rate better than random chance, their accuracy often falls short of the level required for effective identification (Tollmar et al., 2020). This challenge is particularly pronounced among those without training, who find it difficult to recognize the complex security features present in contemporary currency.
In the Philippine context, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) promotes the "Feel, Look, and Tilt" method to help the public verify banknotes. However, the BSP continues to stress the importance of public education on these security features, as unfamiliarity with them increases the likelihood of counterfeit bills circulating undetected (BSP, 2023). A growing concern is that even legitimate banknotes are sometimes misidentified as fake, especially by younger cash handlers who are unfamiliar with older currency designs (Miller, 2024).
Furthermore, research on the capabilities of cashiers and vendors in identifying counterfeit Philippine currency has found that while many routinely check banknotes, a significant portion has never received formal training in counterfeit detection (Santos et al., 2024). The study suggests that structured training programs and increased awareness campaigns are necessary to improve detection accuracy and reduce reliance on manual verification alone.
Given these findings, while manual inspection remains a fundamental method of counterfeit detection, its effectiveness is undermined by the varying levels of knowledge and skill among users. Without proper training, reliance on this method alone may not be sufficient in preventing counterfeit currency from entering circulation.
Following the challenges of manual counterfeit detection, hardware-based systems have emerged as the next major method for verifying the authenticity of banknotes. Among these, ultraviolet (UV) light scanning is one of the most widely used techniques. UV scanners detect security features that are only visible under ultraviolet illumination, such as fluorescent fibers, security threads, and invisible ink markings embedded in legitimate banknotes. These features are designed to glow under UV light, making it easier to differentiate between genuine and counterfeit notes (Sundravadivelu, 2024). Additionally, infrared (IR) scanners are used to analyze banknotes by detecting ink compositions that react differently under infrared exposure, further enhancing counterfeit detection.
Apart from UV and IR scanners, other hardware-based detection methods include magnetic ink detectors and watermark verification devices. Magnetic sensors check for the presence of magnetic properties in the ink used for printing banknotes, as genuine currency often incorporates magnetic components for security. Watermark verification devices, on the other hand, help detect embedded watermark images, which should be visible when the banknote is held against the light (Srilatha, 2024). These methods provide an added layer of security compared to manual inspection, as they rely on measurable physical and chemical properties of authentic banknotes.
However, despite their effectiveness, hardware-based systems have notable limitations. Many counterfeiters have developed techniques to replicate fluorescent and magnetic ink properties, making it possible to produce high-quality forgeries that can bypass UV and magnetic ink detection (Sundravadivelu, 2024). Moreover, these systems are not foolproof; environmental conditions, such as lighting and device calibration, can affect detection accuracy. Another significant drawback is the inefficiency of hardware-based methods for large-scale operations. Businesses and financial institutions handling high volumes of cash require rapid authentication, but hardware-based verification often requires manual intervention and additional processing time. Moreover, these systems are also not ideal for small businesses and private individuals due to their high cost. Many small-scale enterprises and ordinary consumers may find it impractical to invest in expensive detection devices, making them more vulnerable to counterfeit currency circulation (Srilatha, 2024).
Due to the limitations of manual and hardware-based counterfeit detection methods, researchers have increasingly explored mobile-based solutions to enhance accuracy and efficiency. Mobile applications leverage smartphone cameras and computational algorithms to verify banknotes, offering a more accessible and cost-effective alternative to traditional hardware scanners. However, while these technologies show promise, they also face challenges such as environmental dependencies, computational constraints, and a limited focus on specific security features.
Several studies have contributed to the advancement of mobile-based counterfeit detection. Alday (2019) developed a mobile application that utilized the Sobel Edge Detection algorithm to enhance contrast between edges and background areas, making it easier to detect security features like watermarks, micro-lettering, and security threads. This method was particularly applied to high-denomination Philippine banknotes, such as ₱500 and ₱1000, which contain intricate security elements frequently targeted by counterfeiters. However, the effectiveness of this approach was highly dependent on adequate lighting, as poor illumination led to suboptimal edge detection results.
Likewise, Ballado et al. (2015) explored the use of Canny Edge Detection for verifying authenticity through the Optically Variable Device (OVD) patch, a security feature that shifts colors when viewed from different angles. The Canny algorithm, known for its ability to reduce image noise, detect intensity gradients, and trace edges through non-maximum suppression, effectively captured security details. However, the method's reliability declined when banknotes exhibited wear and tear, as physical distortions affected edge-based analysis.
To refine detection techniques, Apoloni et al. (2022) combined Canny Edge Detection with Optical Character Recognition (OCR), achieving a 95.86% accuracy rate. OCR enabled automated extraction and validation of text-based security elements, such as serial numbers and micro-lettering, improving counterfeit detection capabilities. However, this method required precise bill positioning, which posed practical challenges in real-world applications.
More recently, De Goma et al. (2024) proposed an advanced approach by integrating MobileNetv2 and YOLOv5s for feature detection across various Philippine banknotes, including ₱100, ₱200, ₱500, and ₱1000. MobileNetv2, a lightweight deep learning model optimized for mobile devices, allowed for rapid feature extraction while maintaining computational efficiency. Meanwhile, YOLOv5s, a real-time object detection algorithm, provided high-speed and accurate recognition of complex visual patterns. While this integration demonstrated improvements in detection accuracy and processing speed, its reliance on significant computational power posed challenges for widespread adoption, especially on lower-end mobile devices.
Despite these progressions, mobile-based counterfeit detection methods still face common limitations. Many solutions are highly dependent on specific environmental conditions, such as lighting and camera quality, which can affect detection accuracy. Additionally, most studies focus on a limited set of security features, making these approaches vulnerable to evolving counterfeiting techniques. Real-time verification remains a challenge, as mobile applications must balance computational efficiency with detection accuracy to provide instant feedback to users.
To address the persistent challenges of counterfeit detection, BillSense introduces an innovative approach by integrating AI-driven image processing. Unlike previous mobile-based solutions, BillSense utilizes a dataset composed of verified counterfeit and genuine banknotes from both the New Generation Currency (NGC) and Enhanced New Generation Currency (ENGC) series, ensuring a comprehensive and adaptable detection system. By leveraging machine learning algorithms trained on extensive datasets, the application eliminates the need for users to manually adjust lighting conditions or precisely align the bill, enabling real-time counterfeit detection with high accuracy. Furthermore, BillSense enhances user awareness and financial security by highlighting key security features such as watermarks, security threads, optically variable devices (OVDs), and micro-lettering, providing a detailed verification process.
The implementation of BillSense aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 16 (SDG 16), which promotes peace, justice, and strong institutions by reducing financial crimes and enhancing governance. Within this goal, Target 16.4 specifically addresses illicit financial flows and organized crime, including counterfeiting, which is often linked to money laundering and fraudulent activities. By curbing the circulation of counterfeit currency, BillSense contributes to disrupting illicit financial networks, safeguarding economic transactions, and reinforcing financial stability.
Although digital payments are increasingly embraced, cash continues to be the primary method of exchange in the Philippines, as a significant portion of the population still prefers cash transactions. A survey conducted in 2022 revealed that 46% of Filipinos prefer cash over electronic payments, with older age groups demonstrating a stronger preference for cash usage (Statista, 2022). Financial exclusion poses another significant challenge, as nearly 30% of Filipinos remain unbanked, which restricts their ability to participate in digital transactions (Yu, 2024). Furthermore, issues related to internet access and infrastructure complicate the situation, with the country's internet penetration rate standing at only 73.1%, and connectivity problems in rural regions impeding the transition to digital payments (Yu, 2024). Security issues, including fraud and transaction failures, also contribute to users' reluctance to fully embrace cashless payment options (Trout, 2022). Additionally, transaction fees and other expenses associated with digital payments deter lower-income individuals from moving towards cashless transactions, as they perceive insufficient financial benefits (Trout, 2022).
In addition to individual challenges, businesses, and financial institutions encounter obstacles in establishing a completely cashless system. Many small and informal enterprises, which constitute a significant portion of the Philippine economy, lack the necessary infrastructure to facilitate digital transactions (Alvarez et al., 2022). The inconsistent availability of point-of-sale systems and mobile payment technologies further obstructs the smooth adoption of cashless transactions (Alvarez et al., 2022). While 37% of Filipinos believe that the country could transition to a predominantly cashless society by 2030 (Crismundo, 2024), realizing this vision will necessitate substantial advancements in financial literacy, trust in digital systems, and investment in technological infrastructure. Without addressing these critical issues, the Philippines is unlikely to achieve a complete transition to a cashless economy in the foreseeable future.
Given this context, BillSense aims to provide a portable, cost-effective, and user-friendly counterfeit detection solution that ensures financial security, particularly for private individuals and small business owners who are most vulnerable to counterfeit currency fraud. The study specifically seeks to assist end users — especially small business owners — by equipping them with an accessible tool to prevent financial losses and avoid being frequent victims of counterfeit bills.
The BillSense mobile application has the potential to contribute significantly to sustainability across various domains. By providing an accessible and reliable tool for detecting counterfeit bills, it can help reduce financial crimes, leading to a decline in fraud-related incidents and improving overall public trust in cash transactions. This, in turn, can discourage counterfeit-related criminal activities, aiding law enforcement in tracking and preventing such offenses.
Economically, BillSense can protect businesses and consumers from financial losses caused by counterfeit money, ensuring that local economies remain stable and secure. By reducing the circulation of fake bills, the platform helps maintain the integrity of currency, fostering a healthier business environment that encourages growth and investment.
Beyond crime prevention and economic stability, the app also promotes financial literacy by educating users on identifying counterfeit currency, strengthening public awareness of security features in banknotes. This is particularly beneficial for tourists visiting the Philippines, as they may not be familiar with the local currency's security features. BillSense can serve as a reliable guide, helping foreigners avoid counterfeit transactions and ensuring a smoother financial experience during their stay.
On a national scale, BillSense can serve as a data-driven tool for policymakers and financial institutions to enhance currency security measures and combat counterfeiting more effectively. By collecting and analyzing counterfeit reports, authorities can identify high-risk areas, improve law enforcement strategies, and strengthen public confidence in the financial system. As adoption grows, BillSense has the potential to become an essential nationwide platform for safeguarding the Philippine economy against counterfeit-related threats.
chapter1_framework:
CHALLENGES ENCOUNTERED IN DETECTING COUNTERFEIT BILLS
Detecting counterfeit banknotes is a complex task, especially for untrained individuals who rely on manual inspection. The difficulty arises due to uncertainty in distinguishing real from fake notes, cognitive limitations that lead to errors, and the strategies used by counterfeiters to exploit gaps in security. This study integrates theories that may support or explain these challenges, including Signal Detection Theory, Human Error Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, and Routine Activity Theory.
Signal Detection Theory
Signal Detection Theory (SDT) explains how individuals perceive and differentiate signals (genuine banknotes) from noise (counterfeit banknotes) under uncertain conditions. It suggests that decision-making is influenced by both the strength of the signal and external factors such as distractions, experience, and environmental conditions. In counterfeit detection, SDT categorizes outcomes into four possibilities: a correct identification of counterfeit money (hit), a failure to detect counterfeit bills (miss), a false rejection of a real banknote (false alarm), and an accurate recognition of genuine currency (correct rejection)(Lee, 2017).
This theory is highly relevant to the study, as manual counterfeit detection often involves high uncertainty, especially when counterfeit bills closely resemble genuine ones. Users, whether trained professionals or ordinary consumers, may struggle to make accurate judgments due to factors such as poor lighting, time constraints, or lack of familiarity with security features.
Human Error Theory
Human Error Theory highlights the limitations of human cognition, particularly in repetitive or complex tasks. It explains that individuals are prone to making mistakes due to fatigue, distractions, reliance on intuition, or misinterpretation of information (Srilatha, 2024). In counterfeit detection, even experienced individuals, such as bank tellers and cashiers, can fail to identify fake bills, particularly when they are highly sophisticated. This theory suggests that errors occur not necessarily due to incompetence but because of inherent human cognitive constraints. The relevance of this theory to the study lies in the recognition that manual counterfeit detection is prone to human error, thereby affecting one’s judgment.
Cognitive Load Theory
Cognitive Load Theory states that an individual's ability to process and recall information is influenced by three types of cognitive load: intrinsic load (task complexity), extraneous load (unnecessary distractions or poor information presentation), and germane load (the structuring of relevant knowledge for learning). If cognitive load is too high, individuals struggle to make accurate judgments and retain critical information (Sweller, 1988).
In the context of counterfeit detection, individuals with little or no training may find it difficult to distinguish genuine from fake banknotes due to the overwhelming number of details they need to process. Financial professionals, who are accustomed to handling cash, may perform better because they have developed pattern recognition skills over time. This study acknowledges that untrained users experience higher cognitive load, which can reduce detection accuracy.
Routine Activities Theory
Routine Activity Theory explains that crime occurs when three elements converge: a motivated offender, a suitable target, and the absence of a capable guardian (Cohen & Felson, 1979). Counterfeiters are the motivated offenders, cash transactions serve as the suitable targets, and the lack of counterfeit detection tools acts as the absence of a capable guardian.
This theory is particularly relevant to the study as it explains why counterfeiters exploit certain vulnerabilities in financial transactions. Cash-based transactions, particularly in small businesses and informal economies, are prime targets because they lack the verification measures present in banks and large retailers.
KEY FEATURES FACILITATING EFFECTIVE DETECTION OF COUNTERFEITS
To improve counterfeit detection accuracy, technological advancements must integrate advanced image processing and machine learning techniques. The effectiveness of such an application depends on its ability to analyze banknotes in real time, adapt to evolving counterfeit methods, and provide reliable feedback. This study applies Computer Vision Theory to establish a strong technological foundation in proposing a system can accurately detect counterfeit banknotes while remaining efficient and scalable.
Computer Vision Theory
Computer Vision Theory focuses on the use of digital image processing and artificial intelligence to recognize objects and extract meaningful information from images (Apoloni, 2022). This theory is fundamental to the development of BillSense, as the application relies on computer vision techniques such as edge detection, feature extraction, and pattern recognition to analyze banknotes.
The relevance of this theory to the study lies in its application in counterfeit detection. BillSense scans banknotes and identifies key security features such as holograms, serial numbers, and microprinting. By leveraging deep learning algorithms, the app can detect anomalies that are indicative of counterfeiting.

ACCEPTABILITY OF PROPOSED APPLICATION
Beyond technical accuracy, the success of a counterfeit detection application depends on user acceptance and ease of use. If the application is complex or perceived as unnecessary, its adoption will be limited. This study incorporates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to examine factors influencing user acceptance and usability.
Technology Acceptance Model
The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) explains user adoption of new technology based on perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. If users find a system beneficial and easy to operate, they are more likely to adopt it (Ramli, 2024).
This study applies TAM to assess whether users perceive BillSense as a valuable tool for counterfeit detection. If the application is too complex or does not reliably detect counterfeit bills, users may be reluctant to adopt it. By conducting acceptability testing and user feedback surveys, this study will measure whether BillSense meets the criteria for widespread adoption.

chapter2_design:
This study employs a mixed-method research design, integrating both qualitative and quantitative approaches to gain a comprehensive understanding of the research problem. According to Barroga et al (2023), mixed-method research combines elements of both quantitative and qualitative approaches to enhance the breadth and depth of understanding and facilitate collaboration in research. This methodological choice is particularly suitable for this study, as the development of the BillSense mobile application requires both exploratory insights to understand user challenges and empirical validation to assess the application's effectiveness.
The qualitative approach will be used to address Statements of the Problem (SOP) 1 and 2, which focus on understanding the difficulties users face in detecting counterfeit bills and identifying the essential features necessary for an effective detection system. Qualitative research, as defined by Creswell (2014), explores complex phenomena by collecting non-numerical data such as interviews, observations, and open-ended survey responses. This approach is appropriate for uncovering in-depth insights into user experiences, expectations, and the practical challenges of counterfeit detection.
In contrast, the quantitative approach will be applied to SOP 3, which evaluates the acceptability of the developed application. Quantitative research involves the systematic collection and analysis of numerical data to test hypotheses and determine statistical relationships (Creswell & Creswell, 2018). In this study, acceptability metrics such as perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness will be collected through a structured survey. This allows for objective measurement and statistical validation of the application’s effectiveness.
To guide the development of the BillSense mobile application, this study adopts the Design Thinking approach. Design Thinking is a human-centered methodology that prioritizes user needs, iterative prototyping, and real-world testing (Brown, 2009). It is widely used in innovation and product development because it emphasizes problem-solving through empathy, collaboration, and experimentation (Plattner et al., 2010). This approach ensures that the application is designed with direct user input, addressing practical challenges and continuously improving usability based on feedback. Through iterative testing and refinement, the Design Thinking process enhances the application’s effectiveness in actual scenarios by making it more responsive to user needs.
The integration of qualitative and quantitative methods, combined with the Design Thinking framework, provides a holistic perspective in this study. The qualitative approach allows for an in-depth exploration of user challenges and feature requirements, while the quantitative approach ensures empirical validation of the application’s acceptability. Meanwhile, Design Thinking ensures that the mobile application remains user-centered, refining its functionality based on actual user experiences. This methodological framework ensures that BillSense is both practically relevant and scientifically validated, ultimately improving the accuracy and accessibility of counterfeit detection.
chapter2_scope:
This study will focus on the analysis of the “look” and “tilt” security features of Philippine banknotes, specifically targeting only the New Generation Currency (NGC) and Enhanced New Generation Currency (ENGC) series. These banknotes were initially issued in 2010 and 2020, respectively, and remained to be widely circulating in the Philippine economy. The polymer banknotes, which were initially introduced in 2022 with the 1000-peso denomination and subsequently followed in 2024 with the 500-peso, 100-peso, and 50-peso polymer notes, will be excluded from the study.
Although the polymer banknotes possess a well-documented array of security features, there have been no instances of counterfeiting reported for these notes up to the present date of this study, even the 1000-peso polymer note, which has been in circulation since 2022. As a result, there is lack of counterfeit data for comparison with the authentic polymer notes. By concentrating on the NGC and ENGC paper banknotes, particularly 1,000, 500, 200, and 100 denominations which have documented counterfeit examples, the study will be able to provide a comprehensive examination of security features, allowing for significant comparisons between genuine and counterfeit currency.
This study will concentrate on the following security features categorized under the “look” and “tilt” methods of verification. Look features would include watermarks, security fiber, asymmetric serial numbers, and see-through marks. The tilt feature on the other hand comprises of the security thread, concealed value, optically variable ink, optically variable device patch, and enhanced value panel.
The “feel” based security features such as the texture of the security paper and the raised or embossed prints are excluded from the study due to their reliance on tactile inspection which is beyond the technological focus of this research.
Further, the mobile application that will be developed will be designed for Android mobile phones as it is the system that is widely used in the locale. As of March 2025, Android continues to dominate the mobile operating system market in the Philippines, holding a substantial 92.16% share (Stat Counter Global Stats, 2025). In contrast, iOS accounts for 7.74% of the market during the same period. This trend highlights the preference for Android devices among Filipino consumers (Stat Counter Global Stats, 2025).​
chapter2_population:
This study will be conducted in Baguio City, Philippines, a highly urbanized area in northern Luzon known for its cool climate, rich cultural heritage, and thriving tourism industry. The city attracts a significant influx of both local and international tourists, particularly during peak seasons such as the Panagbenga Flower Festival, the Christmas holidays, and other major cultural events. With the increase in commercial transactions during these periods, Baguio City has become a prime target for counterfeit currency circulation (Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, 2023), making it a relevant setting for studying the challenges of counterfeit detection and the usability of an application designed for this purpose.
The banknotes — both authentic and counterfeit — that will be utilized in this study for image processing and transfer learning were sourced from Baguio City. The counterfeit bills were obtained from local businesses and private individuals who had unknowingly encountered them in transactions. Reports of counterfeit banknotes in Baguio City have surfaced, particularly during festive seasons. One notable incident occurred during the Session Road in Bloom event of the Panagbenga Festival, where a vendor was scammed with a fake ₱1,000 bill, prompting the event organizers to issue advisories urging merchants to remain vigilant (SunStar Baguio, 2023). Similarly, during the Christmas Market at the Rose Garden in Burnham Park in 2023, a total of ₱32,000 worth of counterfeit banknotes was detected, raising concerns about the circulation of fake bills during the city's peak tourist and shopping periods (Baguio Midland Courier, 2023). These incidents highlight the real-world impact of counterfeiting, reinforcing the need for an effective detection mechanism, to help businesses and consumers mitigate financial losses.
The population for this study will be carefully selected based on the specific objectives outlined in the statements of the problem (SOP). Given the mixed-method research design, different sampling techniques will be applied, depending on whether the data collection requires exploratory insights (qualitative approach) or measurable validation (quantitative approach) (Creswell & Creswell, 2018).
For SOP 1, which examines the challenges in detecting counterfeit banknotes, participants will include individuals who frequently engage in cash transactions as part of their daily work or business operations. Participants for SOP 1 will be identified through purposive sampling, where individuals who meet the inclusion criteria will be invited to participate (Patton, 2015). Only those who have had firsthand experience or challenges with counterfeit detection will qualify for participation. Further, the number of participants for SOP 1 will be dependent on data saturation but a minimum of five (5) will be interviewed. According to qualitative research on needs assessment, the recommended sample size typically ranges from 5 to 30 participants, depending on the study's focus and the diversity of the participants (Creswell & Poth, 2018). In cases where focus groups are used, a common approach is to include 6 to 10 participants per group to ensure a variety of perspectives are captured (Krueger & Casey, 2015). This range of participants allows researchers to gather meaningful insights while balancing the practicalities of data collection and analysis.

For SOP 2, participants include bank fraud analysts and forensic document examiners with at least two years of experience in financial security and counterfeit detection. This requirement is based on research by Ericsson et al. (1993), which highlights that professionals need at least two years of deliberate practice in a specialized field before they begin developing advanced pattern-recognition skills. In fraud analysis and forensic document examination, recognizing counterfeit currency security features and distinguishing them from genuine banknotes require substantial hands-on experience and training (Kempf & Mierau, 2021).
A study by Schneider et al. (2018) found that forensic document examiners with fewer than two (2) years of experience made twice as many errors when analyzing fraudulent documents compared to those who had been practicing for a longer period. Therefore, requiring at least two years of experience ensures that participants have undergone sufficient exposure, training, and casework, making them qualified to assess the critical security features that should be integrated into the BillSense mobile application.
For SOP 3, which aims to assess the acceptability of the BillSense mobile application, a diverse group of cash-handlers will be involved to evaluate the application’s effectiveness from a user perspective. The respondents will be identified through a proportional quota sampling. Proportional quota sampling is a non-probability sampling method in which researchers categorize the population into specific subgroups and ensure that the sample accurately reflects the proportional representation of each subgroup according to established characteristics. This technique is particularly advantageous when the precise size of the population is unknown, yet it is crucial to uphold the relative proportions of the subgroups. Unlike probability sampling, this method does not necessitate random selection; rather, it guarantees representation by establishing quotas for each subgroup (Etikan & Bala, 2017).
This approach is particularly well-suited for the study at hand, as the participants are organized into three distinct groups (market vendors, small business owners or cashiers, and consumers) making it vital to maintain proportional representation. By employing proportional quota sampling, researchers can prevent any group from being overrepresented or underrepresented, thereby safeguarding the integrity of the results (Acharya et al., 2013). Additionally, given the unavailability of exact population numbers, traditional probability sampling techniques, such as stratified random sampling, become impractical. Proportional quota sampling serves as an effective alternative, enabling researchers to estimate the necessary quotas based on the information at hand while still ensuring a representative sample (Bryman, 2016).

According to Malhotra (2019), market research studies typically require at least 100 participants per key consumer segment to achieve reliable insights and statistical validity. This number ensures that the data collected is representative enough to draw meaningful conclusions about consumer behavior and preferences.
For market vendors and cashiers, a sample size of 50 respondents per group was set. By selecting 50 participants for each of these groups, the study ensures a more stable and reliable dataset for comparisons.
The respondents for the third SOP are the end users, which include market vendors, small business owners or cashiers, and consumers. As the primary users of the BillSense mobile application, their feedback will be essential in evaluating its usability. Their assessment will focus on the app's perceived ease of use and effectiveness in real-world scenarios, particularly in addressing the challenges associated with counterfeit detection during cash transactions.
For general end-users, no minimum years of experience are required because acceptability testing aims to gather insights from a broad range of users, including those with limited expertise in counterfeit detection. Research by Nielsen (1993) suggests that usability and acceptability studies benefit from including the proposed users as they represent real-world consumers who might rely on the app.
